stories.headline: Trump defends Pentagon chief as Massie targets him: 'Hegseth should be praised, not impeached'
stories.note: Trump is standing firmly behind his War Secretary as the impeachment push runs into his full backing.
body: President Trump came to War Secretary Pete Hegseth's defense Monday after outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky launched an effort to impeach the Pentagon chief.

In a Truth Social post, Trump called Massie "a total loser" and pointed to record-high military recruitment and what he called two victories, in Venezuela and Iran, as reasons Hegseth deserves credit instead of impeachment. He urged Congress to "stand up for Pete."
Hegseth reposted the president's message and thanked him, saying "we will never back down." He also said the Pentagon would hold a press conference Tuesday morning.

Massie, in the House since 2012, lost his GOP primary this year to Trump-backed former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein, who went on to win the seat. In a press release, Massie framed his impeachment push as a milder preview of what Democrats will do once they control Congress, and said Trump should replace Hegseth while a successor can still be confirmed. He didn't respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Why it matters: The president is drawing a clear line behind his Pentagon chief, signaling that a lame-duck GOP critic won't get White House cover for an impeachment drive before Democrats take over.

stories.headline: WATCH: Jeffries faces uncertainty from incoming Democrats as House speaker vote approaches
stories.note: Democrats' new majority isn't united behind its own leader before the speaker vote even happens.
body: Several incoming House Democrats won't commit to backing Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for speaker, exposing cracks in the party before it takes control of the House in January.

New Jersey Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, a progressive who recently appeared on Hasan Piker's stream, told Fox News Digital he "hasn't decided yet." Illinois' Patty Garcia said she'd vote with the progressive caucus, DSA member Claire Valdez of New York declined to comment, and Texas' Katie Padilla Stout offered only "I don't know, we'll see." North Carolina's Jamie Ager declined to comment and Missouri's Fred Wellman said he hadn't made up his mind.

Jeffries does have backers. Several incoming members expected to join the Congressional Black Caucus, including Adrian Boafo and Georgia's Jasmine Clark, said they're firmly with him, and Rep. Wesley Bell said he's "Hakeem Jeffries all the way."

Others, like Scott Wiener and Brad Lander, support Jeffries but want an open debate over the party's direction. Lander still predicted Jeffries would be elected overwhelmingly. The caucus picks its nominee next week, with the full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January.
Why it matters: Democrats haven't even been sworn in and their left wing is already holding its own leader at arm's length, a preview of the infighting Republicans can exploit in the new Congress.

stories.headline: SCOTUS allows Trump admin to temporarily resume border construction in Texas' Big Bend
stories.note: The Supreme Court cleared the way for border wall work in Texas to start back up.
body: The Supreme Court on Monday granted the Trump administration's emergency request to restart border wall construction in West Texas, lifting a lower court's hold on the project.

The order pauses a preliminary injunction a federal judge in El Paso issued last month that had stopped work in Customs and Border Protection's Big Bend Sector while the lawsuit plays out. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson noted she would have denied the request but didn't write a dissent.

Environmental groups and local residents sued, arguing DHS moved ahead without congressional authorization and skipped environmental rules. The sector covers more than 500 miles, about a quarter of the southern border, though Reuters reported it accounted for only 1.3% of apprehensions in 2025.

The administration says the wall is key to stopping cartel activity and drug smuggling. Officials said most construction will happen on private land, and Big Bend National Park is slated for a 17-mile barrier without the 30-foot steel fencing used elsewhere.
Why it matters: It's a court win for one of Trump's signature priorities, keeping border wall construction moving even as Democrats prepare to take over Congress.

stories.headline: Arizona Republican holds House seat, surviving re-election scare
stories.note: A home-state GOP win here in Arizona as a Republican hangs on to his House seat.
body: Rep. Eli Crane of Arizona narrowly won a second term, beating Democrat Jonathan Nez in a rematch, the Associated Press projected Monday.

Crane, a former Navy SEAL, also defeated Nez, a former Navajo Nation president, in 2024. This time the margin was 3,834 votes when the race was called, in a seat Fox News Power Rankings had rated Likely Republican. Nez hasn't conceded.
On X, Crane thanked rural Arizonans and his staff and credited Nez for running again. He said he'll "keep fighting against the status quo in Congress."
Trump endorsed Crane as an "America First Patriot" and attacked Nez as a "Radical Left Democrat" who opposed ending taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security.
Why it matters: In a rough cycle for the GOP, Republicans held on to a Trump-backed seat right here in Arizona.

stories.headline: Schumer's grip on power slips as Dems begin to revolt against him, eye new leadership
stories.note: Senate Democrats are fighting among themselves over who should lead them.
body: Chuck Schumer helped Democrats flip the Senate, but a growing number of his colleagues aren't ready to hand him another term as leader.

Schumer has said he plans to run again and become majority leader, which only takes a majority of the caucus. But Sen. Richard Blumenthal told reporters Democrats need "a conversation about leadership" and "new energy and ideas," while admitting he expects Schumer to win because nobody else has stepped up.

Several incoming senators, including Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton and Troy Jackson, have said they won't back Schumer. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a progressive favorite, said nobody should get "a blank check" from the caucus, and Politico reported he's considering a run for the job.
Schumer, on the New York Times' "The Daily" podcast, insisted the caucus is united and focused on moving forward, while warning that if Democrats don't deliver, their gains will disappear.
Why it matters: Instead of a victory lap, Senate Democrats are opening their new majority with a leadership fight that could split moderates from progressives.

stories.headline: Gaza-born Democratic Socialist launches primary bid against Sen John Fetterman
stories.note: The far left is going after one of the few moderate Democrats, deepening the party's split.
body: Ahmed Moor, a 42-year-old Gaza-born member of the Democratic Socialists of America, announced on X that he's challenging Sen. John Fetterman in Pennsylvania's Democratic primary.

Moor said he's running to end the war in Iran and push free healthcare, free childcare and affordable housing, along with "accountability" for what he calls genocide, for ICE and for corruption. His campaign site sharply attacks U.S. aid to Israel.

Fetterman has angered his party's left with his strong support for Israel in its war against Hamas and his willingness to side with Trump on some issues. He hasn't said yet whether he'll run for re-election, and his office didn't immediately respond to Fox News Digital.

According to the Philadelphia Inquirer, Moor came to Pennsylvania as a child, studied at Penn and Harvard, and worked in finance before turning to journalism. He's part of a broader wave of DSA candidates taking on moderate Democrats.
Why it matters: The far left is now targeting one of the few Democrats willing to work with Republicans, a sign the party's socialist wing is gaining confidence and widening its internal split.

stories.headline: Newly elected Dem's blistering GOP attacks emerge after she courted Republican voters: 'Lit on fire'
stories.note: A Democrat who campaigned for Republican votes is now facing her own harsh past attacks on the GOP.
body: South Carolina's Democratic senator-elect Annie Andrews is facing scrutiny as old social media posts trashing Republicans and championing transgender causes resurface after her win.

Andrews, elected in a state Trump carried by about 18 points, ran as a moderate who courted Republicans and independents, even holding a "Republicans and Independents for Annie" town hall and promising to work across the aisle. She also distanced herself from some past positions on transgender issues in a campaign ad.

Her older posts tell a different story. In August 2024 she wrote that the GOP should be "lit on fire & thrown in the dumpster," and she took personal shots at JD Vance and Sen. Katie Britt. She also posted in support of abortion access, drag story hours and tighter gun restrictions.

Independent journalist Zaid Jilani argued Republicans didn't do enough opposition research on Andrews, though NRSC adviser Nathan Brand did highlight her past positions in October. Her campaign didn't respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Why it matters: Andrews' record gives Republicans ammunition to paint her as a partisan who ran away from her own views, a line of attack they can keep using throughout her term.
